nodes.name: Coupling and transport plan
nodes.statement: The random variable $(\bm{x}, \bm{y})$ is referred to as a coupling of $(\mu, \nu)$ and its law, $\gamma$, is called transport plan.

nodes.name: Wasserstein distance between random variables (notation)
nodes.statement: We introduce the following abuse of notation: if $\bm{x} \sim \mu$ and $\bm{y} \sim \nu$, $\wass[p]{\bm{x}}{\bm{y}} \coloneqq \wass[p]{\mu}{\nu}$.

nodes.name: Wasserstein convergence characterization (Villani Theorem 6.9)
nodes.statement: Given $(\bm{x}_n)_{n = 1}^{\infty}$, $\bm{x}$ random variables, then $\lim_{n \to \infty} \wass[p]{\bm{x}_n}{\bm{x}} = 0$ if and only if $\bm{x}_n \xrightarrow{law} \bm{x}$, and $\lim_{n \to \infty} \mean{\norm{\bm{x}_n}^p} = \mean{\norm{\bm{x}}^p}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{W}_p$ convergence is equivalent to convergence in law plus convergence of $p$-th moments.
nodes.label: thm:wassdist

nodes.name: Training dataset
nodes.statement: Consider a supervised learning framework in a regression setting, with a given training dataset $\mathcal{D} \coloneqq \left\{\left(\bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}, i}, \bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}, i}\right)\right\}_{i = 1}^k$, i.e., \begin{equation*} \bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}} \coloneqq \sum_{i = 1}^k \bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}, i} \otimes \bm{e}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}} \times k} \quad \text{and} \quad \bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}} \coloneqq \sum_{i = 1}^k \bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}, i} \otimes \bm{e}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}} \times k}.
nodes.statement_short: Training set $\mathcal{D}$ of $k$ input-output pairs, stacked as matrices $\bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}}$ and $\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$.

nodes.name: Fully connected feed-forward NN
nodes.statement: A fully connected feed-forward NN is defined through an architecture $\bm{\alpha} \coloneqq (\bm{n}, \bm{\varphi})$ with: \begin{enumerate} \item $\bm{n}$ denoting the sizes of the $L + 1$ layers\footnote{An input layer, $L - 1$ hidden layers and an output layer.} (with $L \geq 2$) \begin{equation*} \bm{n} \coloneqq \big(n_0 (\eqcolon d_{\mathrm{in}}), n_1, \dots, n_{L - 1}, n_L (\eqcolon d_{\mathrm{out}})\big), \, n_l \in \mathbb{N}_{> 0}, \, \forall\,\,\,\, l = 0, \dots, L; \end{equation*} \item $\bm{\varphi}$ denoting the $L$ activation functions (applied component-wise) \begin{equation*} \bm{\varphi} \coloneqq (\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_L), \, \varphi_l: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}, \, \forall\,\,\,\, l \in [L], \text{ with } \varphi_1(x) = x, \forall\,\,\,\, x \in \mathbb{R}. \end{equation*} \end{enumerate} In particular, $\forall\,\,\,\, \bm{x}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}}$, the NN is defined as $f(\bm{x}_0) \coloneqq f^{(L)}(\bm{x}_0)$ with \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & f^{(l)}: \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}} \to \mathbb{R}^{n_l}, \ \forall\,\,\,\, l = 0, \dots, L, \\ & f^{(0)}(\bm{x}_0) = \bm{x}_0, \quad f^{(l)}(\bm{x}_0) = \bm{W}^{(l)} \varphi_l\left(f^{(l - 1)}(\bm{x}_0)\right) + \bm{b}^{(l)} \text{ for } l \in [L], \\ \end{aligned} \end{equation} where, for any $l \in [L]$, $\bm{W}^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_l \times n_{l - 1}}$ and $\bm{b}^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_l}$ denote weight matrices and bias vectors, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: An $L$-layer network with widths $\bm{n}$, activations $\bm{\varphi}$, weights $\bm{W}^{(l)}$ and biases $\bm{b}^{(l)}$, defined recursively.
nodes.label: def:nn

nodes.name: Layer recursion of the NN
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & f^{(l)}: \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}} \to \mathbb{R}^{n_l}, \ \forall\,\,\,\, l = 0, \dots, L, \\ & f^{(0)}(\bm{x}_0) = \bm{x}_0, \quad f^{(l)}(\bm{x}_0) = \bm{W}^{(l)} \varphi_l\left(f^{(l - 1)}(\bm{x}_0)\right) + \bm{b}^{(l)} \text{ for } l \in [L], \\ \end{aligned}
nodes.label: eq:nn

nodes.name: Parameter vector and Bayes posterior of a BNN
nodes.statement: By defining $\bm{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^t$ (with $t = \sum_{l = 1}^L n_l (n_{l - 1} + 1)$) the flattened concatenation of all parameters of the NN (both weights and biases), it is possible to apply Bayes' theorem to describe the posterior distribution of a BNN: \begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} p_{\bm{\theta} | \mathcal{D}}(\bm{\theta}) & = \frac{p_{\mathcal{D} | \bm{\theta}}(\mathcal{D}) \, p_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\theta})}{p_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{D})} \propto p_{\bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}}, \bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}} | \bm{\theta}} (\bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}}, \bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}) \, p_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\theta}) \propto p_{\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}} | \bm{\theta}, \bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}}}(\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}) \, p_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\theta}), \end{aligned} \end{equation*} where we assumed that $\bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}}$ is independent of $\bm{\theta}$ and all the random variables admit a density with respect to the Lebesgue measure.
nodes.statement_short: $\bm{\theta}$ is the flattened vector of all weights and biases; Bayes' theorem gives its posterior given $\mathcal{D}$.

nodes.name: Likelihood function
nodes.statement: In particular, if $\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}; \bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}) \coloneqq p_{\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}} | \bm{\theta}, \bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}}}(\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}})$ is the likelihood function then \begin{equation} p_{\bm{\theta} | \mathcal{D}}(\bm{\theta}) \propto \mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}; \bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}) \, p_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\theta}). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The likelihood $\mathcal{L}$ is the density of $\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$ given $\bm{\theta}$; posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior.

nodes.name: Posterior proportional to likelihood times prior
nodes.statement: p_{\bm{\theta} | \mathcal{D}}(\bm{\theta}) \propto \mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}; \bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}) \, p_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\theta}).
nodes.label: eq:bayesbnn

nodes.name: BNN
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a NN (see \cref{eq:nn}) with architecture $\bm{\alpha}$. In order to define a BNN we have to put a prior distribution over $\bm{\theta}$ and a likelihood function $\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}; \bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}})$ for $\bm{\theta}$ associated to the training set $\mathcal{D}$.
differentia: a likelihood function $\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}; \bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}})$ for $\bm{\theta}$ associated to the training set $\mathcal{D}$
nodes.label: def:bnn

nodes.statement: \mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta} | \mathcal{D}} \coloneqq \frac{\mathcal{L}(\cdot; \bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}})}{\int_{\mathbb{R}^S} \mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}; \bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}) d\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\theta})} \mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}},

nodes.name: Gaussian independent prior (Neal prior)
nodes.statement: The prior distribution considered on the parameters is the Gaussian independent prior \citep{neal1996}. Specifically, given the vector of variances $\bm{\sigma} \coloneqq \smash{\big(\big(\sigma_{\bm{W}^{(l)}}^2, \sigma_{\bm{b}^{(l)}}^2\big)\big)_{l = 1}^{L}} \in \left(\mathbb{R}^+ \times \mathbb{R}^+\right)^L$, we assume that \begin{equation} \begin{gathered} \bm{W}^{(l)} \sim \normal{\bm{0}_{n_l \times n_{l - 1}}}{\sigma_{\bm{W}^{(l)}}^2 / n_{l - 1} \, \bm{I}_{n_l \times n_{l - 1}}}, \ \bm{b}^{(l)} \sim \normal{\bm{0}_{n_l}}{\sigma_{\bm{b}^{(l)}}^2 \bm{I}_{n_l}}, \text{ for } l \in [L]. \end{gathered} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Weights are i.i.d. Gaussian with variance $\sigma_W^2/n_{l-1}$, biases Gaussian with variance $\sigma_b^2$, given the variance vector $\bm{\sigma}$.

nodes.name: Neal Gaussian prior on weights and biases
nodes.statement: \begin{gathered} \bm{W}^{(l)} \sim \normal{\bm{0}_{n_l \times n_{l - 1}}}{\sigma_{\bm{W}^{(l)}}^2 / n_{l - 1} \, \bm{I}_{n_l \times n_{l - 1}}}, \ \bm{b}^{(l)} \sim \normal{\bm{0}_{n_l}}{\sigma_{\bm{b}^{(l)}}^2 \bm{I}_{n_l}}, \text{ for } l \in [L]. \end{gathered}
nodes.label: eq:nealprior

nodes.name: Network output on an input set
nodes.statement: In particular, we need to retrace the well-known results which state that the asymptotic distribution of $f_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{x}) \coloneqq \sum_{i = 1}^m f_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{x}_i) \otimes \bm{e}_i$ converges to the neural network Gaussian process (NNGP), where $\bm{x} = \{\bm{x}_i\}_{i = 1}^m$, $m \in \mathbb{N}_{> 0}$, is a generic input set.

nodes.name: Compact form of BNN layers
nodes.statement: In order to have a simpler description of the subsequent theory it is convenient to write the layers of the BNNs in a compact form: $f^{(0)}_{\bm{\theta}}: \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}} \times m} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}} \times m}$, $f^{(0)}_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{x}) = \bm{x}$ and for every $l \in [L]$, $f^{(l)}_{\bm{\theta}}: \mathbb{R}^{n_{l - 1} \times m} \to \mathbb{R}^{n_l \times m}$, \begin{align*} f^{(l)}_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{x}) & = \sum_{i = 1}^m f^{(l)}_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{x}_i) \otimes \bm{e}_i = \sum_{i = 1}^m \bm{W}^{(l)} \varphi_l\left(f^{(l - 1)}_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{x}_i)\right) \otimes \bm{e}_i + \bm{b}^{(l)} \otimes \bm{1}_{m} = \\ & = \left(\bm{W}^{(l)} \otimes \bm{I}_{m}\right) \varphi_l\left(f^{(l - 1)}_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{x})\right) + \bm{b}^{(l)} \otimes \bm{1}_{m}, \end{align*} where $\bm{W}^{(l)} \otimes \bm{I}_{m} \in \mathbb{R}^{(n_l \times n_{l - 1}) \times (m \times m)}$ should be thought as an element of $\mathbb{R}^{(n_l \times m) \times (n_{l - 1} \times m)}$. We define $f_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{x}) \coloneqq f^{(L)}_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{x})$.
nodes.statement_short: Layers written on the whole input set at once via Kronecker products; $f_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{x})$ is the last layer.
nodes.label: rem:nncompact

nodes.name: Gaussian process
nodes.statement: Let $H = (H(\bm{x}_0))_{\bm{x}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}}}$ be a stochastic process such that for any $\bm{x}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}}$, $H(\bm{x}_0)$ is a random vector with values in $\left(\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}}, \borel{\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}}}\right)$. Then $H$ is said to be a Gaussian process with mean function $\bm{M}: \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}}$ and covariance kernel $\bm{H}: \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}} \times \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}} \times d_{\mathrm{out}}}$, if for any $m > 0$, given $\bm{x} = (\bm{x}_i)_{i = 1}^m \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}} \times m}$, \begin{equation*} H(\bm{x}) \coloneqq \left(H(\bm{x}_1), \dots, H(\bm{x}_m)\right) \sim \normal{\bm{M}(\bm{x})}{\bm{H}(\bm{x})}, \end{equation*} where \begin{equation*} \bm{M}(\bm{x}) = \left(\bm{M}(\bm{x}_1), \dots, \bm{M}(\bm{x}_m)\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}} \times m}, \end{equation*} and $\bm{H}(\bm{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^{(d_{\mathrm{out}} \times m) \times (d_{\mathrm{out}} \times m)}$ can be viewed as a block matrix with $m \times m$ blocks such that, for any $i, j \in [m]^2$, the block $(i, j)$ of $\bm{H}(\bm{x})$ is $\left(\bm{H}(\bm{x})\right)_{i, j} = \bm{H}(\bm{x}_i, \bm{x}_j) \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}} \times d_{\mathrm{out}}}$. For such $H$ we set $H \sim \mathcal{GP}\left(\bm{M}, \bm{H}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: A process whose finite-dimensional marginals are Gaussian with mean $\bm{M}(\bm{x})$ and block covariance $\bm{H}(\bm{x})$; written $\mathcal{GP}(\bm{M},\bm{H})$.
nodes.label: def:gp

nodes.name: Student-t process
nodes.statement: In analogy with \Cref{def:gp} it is possible to define Student-$t$ processes replacing the condition on the distribution of $H(\bm{x})$ with a multivariate Student-$t$ with $a$ degrees of freedom: $H(\bm{x}) \sim \tstud{a}{\bm{M}(\bm{x})}{\bm{H}(\bm{x})}$, $a > 0$.

nodes.name: Infinite-width layer laws and NNGP kernels
nodes.statement: Following \citet{matthews2018} and \citet{lee2018}, we report below the laws of the random matrices $(G^{(l)}(\bm{x}))_{l = 1}^L$ associated with the infinite-width limits of the $L$ hidden layers of a BNN, evaluated on the input set $\bm{x}$, deriving general expressions for their corresponding Gaussian processes, $(G^{(l)})_{l = 1}^L$: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & G^{(0)}(\bm{x}) \coloneqq \bm{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}} \times m} \text{ constant r.v.}, \\ & G^{(l)}(\bm{x}) \sim \normal{\bm{0}_{n_l \times m}}{\bm{I}_{n_l} \otimes \bm{K}^{(l)}(\bm{x})}, \text{ with } \bm{K}^{(l)}(\bm{x}) \coloneqq \left(\bm{K}^{(l)}(\bm{x}_i, \bm{x}_j)\right)_{i, j \in [m] \times [m]}, \end{aligned} \end{equation} and, $\forall\,\,\,\, \bm{x}_0, \bm{x}'_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}}$, $\forall\,\,\,\, l = 2, \dots, L$, \begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} & \bm{K}^{(1)}(\bm{x}_0, \bm{x}'_0) \coloneqq \sigma_{\bm{W}^{(1)}}^2 (\bm{x}_0^T \bm{x}'_0) / d_{\mathrm{in}} + \sigma_{\bm{b}^{(1)}}^2, \\ & \bm{K}^{(l)}(\bm{x}_0, \bm{x}'_0) \coloneqq \sigma_{\bm{W}^{(l)}}^2 \mean{\varphi_{l}\left(G^{(l - 1)}(\bm{x}_0)_1\right) \varphi_{l}\left(G^{(l - 1)}(\bm{x}'_0)_1\right)} + \sigma_{\bm{b}^{(l)}}^2. \end{aligned} \end{equation*}
nodes.origin_citation: Matthews et al. 2018; Lee et al. 2018
nodes.statement_short: Limiting hidden-layer laws $G^{(l)}(\bm{x})$ are centered Gaussians with covariance $\bm{I}_{n_l}\otimes\bm{K}^{(l)}(\bm{x})$, kernels defined recursively.

nodes.name: Laws of the limiting layers
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & G^{(0)}(\bm{x}) \coloneqq \bm{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}} \times m} \text{ constant r.v.}, \\ & G^{(l)}(\bm{x}) \sim \normal{\bm{0}_{n_l \times m}}{\bm{I}_{n_l} \otimes \bm{K}^{(l)}(\bm{x})}, \text{ with } \bm{K}^{(l)}(\bm{x}) \coloneqq \left(\bm{K}^{(l)}(\bm{x}_i, \bm{x}_j)\right)_{i, j \in [m] \times [m]}, \end{aligned}
nodes.label: eq:nngpx

nodes.name: Layer-wise asymptotic Gaussian processes
nodes.statement: From \cref{eq:nngpx} it is possible to define the asymptotic Gaussian processes of each hidden layer, $l \in [L]$, as \begin{equation} G^{(l)} = (G^{(l)}(\bm{x}_0))_{\bm{x}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}}} \quad \text{and} \quad G^{(l)} \sim \mathcal{GP}\left(\bm{0}, \bm{I}_{n_l} \otimes \bm{K}^{(l)}\right). \end{equation}
nodes.origin_citation: Matthews et al. 2018; Lee et al. 2018

nodes.name: Asymptotic Gaussian process of layer l
nodes.statement: G^{(l)} = (G^{(l)}(\bm{x}_0))_{\bm{x}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}}} \quad \text{and} \quad G^{(l)} \sim \mathcal{GP}\left(\bm{0}, \bm{I}_{n_l} \otimes \bm{K}^{(l)}\right).
nodes.label: eq:nngp

nodes.name: Last-layer NNGP and kernel notation
nodes.statement: In analogy with the notation introduced for $f_{\bm{\theta}}$ we define $G(\bm{x}) \coloneqq G^{(L)}(\bm{x})$ and $\bm{K}(\bm{x}) \coloneqq \bm{K}^{(L)}(\bm{x})$.

nodes.name: NNGP
nodes.statement: We refer to $G = (G(\bm{x}_0))_{\bm{x}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}}}$ as the NNGP associated to a BNN with architecture $\bm{\alpha}$ and vector of variances $\bm{\sigma}$.

nodes.name: Quantitative CLT for prior BNNs
nodes.statement: Let $f_{\bm{\theta}}$ BNN, with architecture $\bm{\alpha} = (\bm{n}, \bm{\varphi})$, $\bm{\varphi}$ collection of Lipschitz activation functions, a prior on $\bm{\theta}$ as in \cref{eq:nealprior}, $\left(G^{(l)}\right)_{l = 1}^L$ Gaussian processes as in \cref{eq:nngp} and an input set $\bm{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in} \times m}}$. Then, $\forall\,\,\,\, l \in [L]$ exists a constant $c > 0$ independent of $\left(n_j\right)_{j = 1}^l$, such that, \begin{equation} \wass[p]{f_{\bm{\theta}}^{(l)}(\bm{x})}{G^{(l)}(\bm{x})} \leq c \sqrt{n_l} \sum_{j = 1}^{l - 1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{n_j}}. \end{equation}
conclusions: $\forall\,\,\,\, l \in [L]$ exists a constant $c > 0$ independent of $\left(n_j\right)_{j = 1}^l$, such that,

nodes.name: Faster convergence under Gaussian prior
nodes.statement: We can observe that in \Cref{fig:gaussianprior}, i.e., under Gaussian prior, the convergence is much faster and more precise compared to the Gaussian-Inverse-Gamma prior case (\Cref{fig:normalinvgammaprior}). This behavior, while likely influenced by our specific sampling procedure for the posterior BNNs, is also consistent with theoretical expectations. Indeed, although the theoretical convergence rates of the limiting processes are identical for both the Gaussian prior and the Gaussian-Inverse-Gamma prior cases (see \Cref{cor:convposterior} and \Cref{thm:studposterior}), the associated multiplicative constants differ significantly in magnitude. Therefore, given a common fixed width, different distances between the posterior BNNs and their limiting processes are to be expected.
nodes.statement_short: Convergence looks faster under the fixed-variance Gaussian prior: rates agree but multiplicative constants differ.

nodes.name: Student-t process models data variance more accurately
nodes.statement: The posterior Student-$t$ process models the variance of the data more accurately compared to the posterior Gaussian process. This is an expected behavior, as the Gaussian-Inverse-Gamma model explicitly estimates the data variance during the Bayesian learning, whereas no such estimation is performed when we use a Gaussian prior. This final result also highlights that using a Gaussian-Inverse-Gamma prior provides a more accurate representation of the data, particularly in scenarios in which the dataset is relatively small.
nodes.statement_short: Empirically the posterior Student-$t$ process captures data variance better than the posterior GP, since the model estimates the variance.

nodes.name: Tensor space R^S
nodes.statement: Given $S$ finite set (e.g., $[n] \text{ or } [n_1] \times \dots \times [n_k], \text{ for some } k \geq 2$, where $[n] =$ $= \{1, \dots, n\}$) we denote with $\mathbb{R}^S$ the vector space of real valued functions $\bm{v}: S \to \mathbb{R}$ (column vectors which generalizes to multidimensional tensors).

nodes.name: Canonical basis, ones and zero tensors
nodes.statement: We adopt the notation $\bm{v}_s \coloneqq \bm{v}(s)$, $\forall\,\,\,\, s \in S$, and we introduce the following conventions: $\bm{e}_s$ is the $s$\textsuperscript{th} vector of the canonical base ($\bm{e}_s(s) = 1$ and $\bm{e}_s(r) = 0$, $\forall\,\,\,\, r \in S \setminus \{s\}$), $\bm{1}_{S} \coloneqq \sum_{s \in S} \bm{e}_s$ and $\bm{0}_{S}$ is the constant null vector.

nodes.name: Tensors as linear maps
nodes.statement: Given $S$, $T$ two finite sets, we can see the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{S \times T}$ as the space of linear transformations $\bm{A}: \mathbb{R}^T \to \mathbb{R}^S$, defining \begin{equation*} \forall\,\,\,\, \bm{v} \in \mathbb{R}^T, \, \bm{A} \bm{v} \coloneqq \bm{A}(\bm{v}) = \sum_{s \in S} \left(\sum_{t \in T} \bm{A}_{s, t} \bm{v}_t\right) \bm{e}_s. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Symmetric linear transformations
nodes.statement: If $S = T$, we introduce the notation $\operatorname{Sym}^{S}$ for the set of symmetric linear transformations in $\mathbb{R}^{S \times S}$, i.e., $\bm{A} \in \operatorname{Sym}^{S}$ if and only if $\bm{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{S \times S}$, $\bm{A} = \bm{A}^T$.

nodes.name: Symmetric positive definite matrices
nodes.statement: Moreover, we denote with $\operatorname{Sym}_+^{S}$ the subset of $\operatorname{Sym}^{S}$ composed by symmetric, positive definite matrices, where a matrix $\bm{A}$ is said to be positive definite if $\forall\,\,\,\, \bm{v} \in \mathbb{R}^S \setminus \{0\}$, $\bm{v}^T \bm{A} \bm{v} > 0$.

nodes.name: Outer (tensor) product
nodes.statement: We define the outer product (or tensor product) between $\bm{v} \in \mathbb{R}^S$ and $\bm{w} \in \mathbb{R}^{T}$ as $\bm{v} \otimes \bm{w} \in \mathbb{R}^{S \times T}$ with $(\bm{v} \otimes \bm{w})_{s, t} \coloneqq \bm{v}_s \bm{w}_t$, $\forall\,\,\,\, s \in S, t \in T$, denoting $\bm{v} \otimes \bm{v}$ as $\bm{v}^{\otimes 2}$.

nodes.name: Identity map
nodes.statement: We also define the identity map $\bm{I}_S: \mathbb{R}^S \to \mathbb{R}^S$ as $\bm{I}_S \coloneqq \sum_{s \in S} \bm{e}_s^{\otimes 2}$, observing that, $\forall\,\,\,\, \bm{v} \in \mathbb{R}^S$, $\bm{I}_S \bm{v} = \sum_{s \in S} (\sum_{t \in S} (\bm{I}_S)_{s, t} \bm{v}_t) \bm{e}_s =$ $= \sum_{s \in S} \bm{v}_s \bm{e}_s = \bm{v}$.

nodes.name: Standard scalar product
nodes.statement: Given a generic pair of elements in a real vector space, $\bm{v}, \bm{w} \in \mathbb{R}^S$, we define the standard scalar product between them as \begin{equation*} \langle \bm{v}, \bm{w} \rangle \coloneqq \trace{\bm{v} \otimes \bm{w}} = \sum_{s \in S} \bm{v}_s \bm{w}_s. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Euclidean norm
nodes.statement: Analogously we can define the Euclidean norm (or $2$-norm) induced by the scalar product as \begin{equation} \norm{\bm{v}} = \langle \bm{v}, \bm{v} \rangle^{1/2} = \left(\sum_{s \in S} \bm{v}_s^2\right)^{1/2}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Euclidean norm of a tensor
nodes.statement: \norm{\bm{v}} = \langle \bm{v}, \bm{v} \rangle^{1/2} = \left(\sum_{s \in S} \bm{v}_s^2\right)^{1/2}.

nodes.name: p-norm

nodes.name: Random variable
nodes.statement: Given $S$ finite set, a random variable $\bm{x}$ with values in $\mathbb{R}^S$ is a measurable map \begin{equation*} \bm{x}: (\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mathbb{P}) \to (\mathbb{R}^S, \borel{\mathbb{R}^S}). \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Law of a random variable
nodes.statement: We denote with $\mathbb{P}_{\bm{x}}$ the distribution (or law) of $\bm{x}$, \begin{equation*} \mathbb{P}_{\bm{x}} \coloneqq \prob{\bm{x}^{-1}(A)}, \, \forall\,\,\,\, A \in \borel{\mathbb{R}^S}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Mean and variance
nodes.statement: Given $\bm{x}$ random variable with values on $\mathbb{R}^S$ we define its mean value, or first moment, and its variance\footnote{Often referred as covariance if $|S| > 1$.}, or second moment of $\bm{x} - \mean{\bm{x}}$, respectively as \begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} \mean{\bm{x}} & \coloneqq \left(\mean{\bm{x}_s}\right)_{s \in S} = \left(\int_{\Omega} \bm{x}_s(\omega) d\mathbb{P}(\omega)\right)_{s \in S} \in \mathbb{R}^S, \end{aligned} \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} \var{\bm{x}} & \coloneqq \mean{\left(\bm{x} - \mean{\bm{x}}\right)^{\otimes 2}} \in \operatorname{Sym}_+^{S}. \end{aligned} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Lebesgue norm of a random variable
nodes.statement: Given $p \geq 1$, we define the Lebesgue norm of order $p$ of $\bm{x}$ as \begin{equation*} \norm{\bm{x}}_{L^p} \coloneqq \mean{\norm{\bm{x}}^p}^{1/p} \in \mathbb{R}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Gaussian random variable
nodes.statement: Given $\bm{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^S$, $\bm{\Sigma} \in \operatorname{Sym}_+^{S}$, we denote with $\normal{\bm{\mu}}{\bm{\Sigma}}$ the distribution of a Gaussian random variable $\bm{x}: (\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mathbb{P}) \to (\mathbb{R}^S, \borel{\mathbb{R}^S})$, such that \begin{equation*} \mean{\bm{x}} = \bm{\mu} \quad \text{and} \quad \var{\bm{x}} = \mean{\left(\bm{x} - \bm{\mu}\right)^{\otimes 2}} = \bm{\Sigma}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Inverse-Gamma distribution
nodes.statement: A random variable $s$, with values in $\left(\mathbb{R}^+, \borel{\mathbb{R}^+}\right)$, is said to be Inverse-Gamma distributed with parameters $a$ and $b$ in $\mathbb{R}^+$ (denoted as $s \sim \invgamma{a}{b}$), if $\mathbb{P}_{s}$ admits a density with respect to the Lebesgue measure $\lambda^+$ on $\mathbb{R}^+$, and in particular \begin{equation*} p_s(s) \coloneqq \frac{d\mathbb{P}_{s}}{d\lambda^+}(s) = \frac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)} \left(\frac{1}{s}\right)^{a + 1} \exp{-\frac{b}{s}}. \end{equation*}

Given the Bayesian framework presented in \cref{eq:hiervariancenngp,eq:hiermodel,eq:rescaledkernel}, in order to get the posterior distribution of $G( m{x}_{\mathcal{D}}) \, | \, \mathcal{D}$ we write explicitly all the densities and apply the Bayes rule. In particular, assuming $ m{K}'( m{x}_{\mathcal{D}}) \in \operatorname{Sym}_+^{k}$ invertible (we already know that is symmetric positive semi-definite), flattening all the random matrices by columns and defining  egin{equation*}  m{y}_{\mathrm{f}} \coloneqq  latten{ m{y}_{\mathcal{D}}}, \quad  m{z}_{\mathrm{f}} \coloneqq  latten{ m{z}}, \end{equation*} with $ m{z} \coloneqq G( m{x}_{\mathcal{D}}) \in \mathbb{R}^{n_L 	imes k}$, we get  egin{equation*}  egin{aligned} p_{G( m{x}_{\mathcal{D}}) | \sigma^2}( m{z}) & =  rac{1}{\left((2\pi \sigma^2)^{n_L k} \det{ m{K}'( m{x}_{\mathcal{D}}) \otimes_K  m{I}_{n_L}}ight)^{1/2}} \cdot \ & \kern14.65pt \cdot \exp{- rac{1}{2\sigma^2}  m{z}_{\mathrm{f}}^T \left( m{K}'( m{x}_{\mathcal{D}}) \otimes_K  m{I}_{n_L}ight)^{-1}  m{z}_{\mathrm{f}}}, \ p_{\sigma^2}(\sigma^2) & =  rac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)}  rac{1}{\left(\sigma^2ight)^{a + 1}} \exp{- rac{b}{\sigma^2}}, \ p_{ m{y}_{\mathcal{D}} | G( m{x}_{\mathcal{D}}), \sigma^2}( m{y}_{\mathcal{D}}) &=  rac{1}{\left(2\pi\sigma^2ight)^{n_L k / 2}} \exp{- rac{1}{2 \sigma^2} ( m{y}_{\mathrm{f}} -  m{z}_{\mathrm{f}})^T ( m{y}_{\mathrm{f}} -  m{z}_{\mathrm{f}})}. \end{aligned} \end{equation*} with $\otimes_K$ representing the Kronecker product. \ By performing explicit computation we retrieve the posterior distribution of $G( m{x}_{\mathcal{D}}), \sigma^2 \, | \, \mathcal{D}$ as  egin{equation*}  egin{aligned} p_{G( m{x}_{\mathcal{D}}), \sigma^2 | \mathcal{D}}( m{z}, \sigma^2) & \propto p_{ m{y}_{\mathcal{D}} | G( m{x}_{\mathcal{D}}), \sigma^2}( m{y}_{\mathcal{D}}) \, p_{G( m{x}_{\mathcal{D}}) | \sigma^2}( m{z}) \, p_{\sigma^2}(\sigma^2) \propto \ & \propto  rac{1}{\left(\sigma^2ight)^{n_L k / 2}} \exp{- rac{1}{2\sigma^2} ( m{y}_{\mathrm{f}} -  m{z}_{\mathrm{f}})^T ( m{y}_{\mathrm{f}} -  m{z}_{\mathrm{f}})} \cdot \ & \kern14.65pt \cdot  rac{1}{\left(\sigma^2ight)^{n_L k / 2} \sqrt{\det{ m{K}'( m{x}_{\mathcal{D}})}}} \exp{- rac{1}{2 \sigma^2}  m{z}_{\mathrm{f}}^T \left( m{K}'( m{x}_{\mathcal{D}}) \otimes_K  m{I}_{n_L}ight)^{-1}  m{z}_{\mathrm{f}}} \cdot \ & \kern14.65pt \cdot  rac{1}{\left(\sigma^2ight)^{a + 1}} \exp{- rac{b}{\sigma^2}}. \end{aligned} \end{equation*} Defining $ m{N} \coloneqq  m{K}'( m{x}_{\mathcal{D}}) \otimes_K  m{I}_{n_1} \in \operatorname{Sym}_+^{n_1 k}$, $ m{M} \coloneqq  m{I}_{n_1 k} +  m{N}^{-1} \in \operatorname{Sym}_+^{n_1 k}$, through simple manipulations of the exponent we get  egin{equation*}  egin{aligned} & ( m{y}_{\mathrm{f}} -  m{z}_{\mathrm{f}})^T ( m{y}_{\mathrm{f}} -  m{z}_{\mathrm{f}}) +  m{z}_{\mathrm{f}}^T  m{N}^{-1}  m{z}_{\mathrm{f}} = 
orm{ m{y}_{\mathrm{f}}}_2^2 + 
orm{ m{z}_{\mathrm{f}}}_2^2 - 2  m{y}_{\mathrm{f}}^T  m{z}_{\mathrm{f}} +  m{z}_{\mathrm{f}}^T  m{N}^{-1}  m{z}_{\mathrm{f}} = \ & \kern20pt =  m{z}_{\mathrm{f}}^T \left( m{I}_{n_L k} +  m{N}^{-1}ight)  m{z}_{\mathrm{f}} - 2  m{y}_{\mathrm{f}}^T  m{z}_{\mathrm{f}} +  m{y}_{\mathrm{f}}^T  m{y}_{\mathrm{f}} \pm  m{y}_{\mathrm{f}}^T \left( m{I}_{n_L k} +  m{N}^{-1}ight)^{-1}  m{y}_{\mathrm{f}} = \ & \kern20pt =  m{z}_{\mathrm{f}}^T  m{M}  m{z}_{\mathrm{f}} - 2  m{y}_{\mathrm{f}}^T  m{z}_{\mathrm{f}} +  m{y}_{\mathrm{f}}^T  m{y}_{\mathrm{f}} \pm  m{y}_{\mathrm{f}}^T  m{M}^{-1}  m{y}_{\mathrm{f}} = \ & \kern20pt = \left( m{z}_{\mathrm{f}} -  m{M}^{-1}  m{y}_{\mathrm{f}}ight)^T  m{M} \left( m{z}_{\mathrm{f}} -  m{M}^{-1}  m{y}_{\mathrm{f}}ight) +  m{y}_{\mathrm{f}}^T \left( m{I}_{n_L k} -  m{M}^{-1}ight)  m{y}_{\mathrm{f}}. \end{aligned} \end{equation*} Substituting and multiplying for the constant term $\sqrt{\det{ m{M}^{-1}}}$ we obtain  egin{equation}  egin{aligned} p_{G( m{x}_{\mathcal{D}}), \sigma^2 | \mathcal{D}}( m{z}, \sigma^2) & \propto  rac{1}{\left(\sigma^2ight)^{n_L k / 2} \sqrt{\det{ m{M}^{-1}}}} \exp{- rac{1}{2 \sigma^2} ( m{z}_{\mathrm{f}} -  m{M}^{-1}  m{y}_{\mathrm{f}})^T  m{M} ( m{z}_{\mathrm{f}} -  m{M}^{-1}  m{y}_{\mathrm{f}})} \cdot \ & \kern14.65pt \cdot  rac{1}{\left(\sigma^2ight)^{(a + n_L k / 2) + 1}} \exp{- rac{1}{\sigma^2} \left(b +  rac{1}{2} \left( m{y}_{\mathrm{f}}^T \left( m{I}_{n_L k} -  m{M}^{-1}ight)  m{y}_{\mathrm{f}}ight)ight)}. \end{aligned} \end{equation} From \cref{eq:marginalposteriors} it is possible to identify two kernels: one associable with a Gaussian density and the other with an Inverse-Gamma density,  egin{equation*}  egin{aligned}  latten{G( m{x}_{\mathcal{D}})} \, | \, \sigma^2, \mathcal{D} & \sim 
ormal{ m{M}^{-1}  latten{ m{y}_{\mathcal{D}}}}{\sigma^2  m{M}^{-1}}, \ \sigma^{2} \, | \, \mathcal{D} & \sim \invgamma{a +  rac{n_L k}{2}}{b +  rac{1}{2} \left( latten{ m{y}_{\mathcal{D}}}^T \left( m{I}_{n_1 k} -  m{M}^{-1}ight)  latten{ m{y}_{\mathcal{D}}}ight)}. \end{aligned} \end{equation*} This result allows us to apply the following \Cref{lem:norminvgammastudent} (see \citet{bayesiantheory2009}) and state that the induced posterior distribution, $G( m{x}_{\mathcal{D}}) \, | \, \mathcal{D}$ is a $(n_L 	imes k)$-dimensional Student-$t$:  egin{equation*}  egin{aligned}  latten{G( m{x}_{\mathcal{D}})} \, | \, \mathcal{D} \sim 	stud{2a + n_L k}{ m{\mu}_{\mathrm{post}}}{ m{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{post}}}, \end{aligned} \end{equation*} with  egin{equation*}  egin{aligned}  m{M} & \coloneqq  m{I}_{n_L k} + \left( m{K}'( m{x}) \otimes_K  m{I}_{n_L}ight)^{-1}, \  m{\mu}_{\mathrm{post}} & \coloneqq  m{M}^{-1}  latten{ m{y}_{\mathcal{D}}}, \  m{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{post}} & \coloneqq \left(b +  rac{1}{2} \left( latten{ m{y}_{\mathcal{D}}}^T \left( m{I}_{n_L k} -  m{M}^{-1}ight)  latten{ m{y}_{\mathcal{D}}}ight)ight)  rac{2}{2a + n_L k}  m{M}^{-1}. \end{aligned} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Write all densities, complete the square in the exponent to separate a Gaussian and an Inverse-Gamma kernel, then marginalize with Lemma B.1.

nodes.name: Gaussian-Inverse-Gamma marginal is Student-t
nodes.statement: Let $k \in \mathbb{N}_{> 0}$, and $(\bm{z}, \sigma^2)$ Gaussian-Inverse-Gamma (Gaussian-IG) distributed, i.e., \begin{align*} \bm{z} \, | \, \sigma^2 & \sim \normal{\bm{\mu}}{\sigma^2 \bm{\Lambda}} \text{ with } \bm{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^k, \, \bm{\Lambda} \in \operatorname{Sym}_+^{k} \text{ and} \\ \sigma^2 & \sim \invgamma{\alpha}{\beta} \text{ with } \alpha, \beta > 0, \end{align*} then $\bm{z}$ is distributed as a $k$-dimensional Student-$t$ with $2 \alpha$ degrees of freedom, $\bm{z} \sim \tstud{2\alpha}{\bm{\mu}}{\frac{\beta}{\alpha} \bm{\Lambda}}$.
conclusions: $\bm{z}$ is distributed as a $k$-dimensional Student-$t$ with $2 \alpha$ degrees of freedom, $\bm{z} \sim \tstud{2\alpha}{\bm{\mu}}{\frac{\beta}{\alpha} \bm{\Lambda}}$
nodes.statement_short: If $z|\sigma^2$ is Gaussian with covariance $\sigma^2\Lambda$ and $\sigma^2$ is Inverse-Gamma, then $z$ is multivariate Student-$t$.
nodes.label: lem:norminvgammastudent

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma B.1
nodes.statement: We know, by hypothesis that $(\bm{z}, \sigma^2)$ is such that \begin{align*} p_{(\bm{z}, \sigma^2)}(\bm{z}, \sigma^2) & = \frac{1}{(2 \pi)^{\frac{k}{2}} \left(\sigma^2\right)^{\frac{k}{2}} \sqrt{\det{\bm{\Lambda}}}} \exp{-\frac{1}{2 \sigma^2} (\bm{z} - \bm{\mu})^T \bm{\Lambda}^{-1} (\bm{z} - \bm{\mu})} \cdot \\ & \kern14.65pt \cdot \frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)} \left(\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\right)^{\alpha + 1} \exp{-\frac{\beta}{\sigma^2}}. \end{align*} Marginalizing over the variance $\sigma^2$ we get \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} p_{\bm{z}}(\bm{z}) & = \int_{0}^{\infty} p_{(\bm{z}, \sigma^2)}(\bm{z}, \sigma^2) d \sigma^2 = \\ & \propto \int_{0}^{\infty} \exp{-\frac{1}{2 \sigma^2} \left(2 \beta + (\bm{z} - \bm{\mu})^T \bm{\Lambda}^{-1} (\bm{z} - \bm{\mu})\right)} \left(\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\right)^{\alpha + \frac{k}{2} + 1} d \sigma^2. \end{aligned} \end{equation} Setting $a = \alpha + \frac{k}{2}$, $b = \frac{2 \beta + (\bm{z} - \bm{\mu})^T \bm{\Lambda}^{-1} (\bm{z} - \bm{\mu})}{2}$, $s = \sigma^2$ one can rewrite the last line of \cref{eq:ninvgstud1} as \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} p_{\bm{z}}(\bm{z}) & \propto \int_{0}^{\infty} s^{-(a + 1)} \exp{-\frac{b}{s}} d s = \int_{\infty}^{0} \left(\frac{t}{b}\right)^{a + 1} e^{-t} \left(-\frac{b}{t^2}\right) dt = \\ & = \int_{0}^{\infty} b^{-a} t^{a - 1} e^{-t} dt = \Gamma(a) b^{-a} \propto \left(\frac{2 \beta + (\bm{z} - \bm{\mu})^T \bm{\Lambda}^{-1} (\bm{z} - \bm{\mu})}{2}\right)^{-\left(\alpha + \frac{k}{2}\right)} \propto \\ & \propto \left(1 + \frac{1}{2 \alpha} (\bm{z} - \bm{\mu})^T \left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha} \bm{\Lambda}\right)^{-1} (\bm{z} - \bm{\mu})\right)^{-\frac{2\alpha + k}{2}}, \end{aligned} \end{equation} where in the first equality of \cref{eq:ninvgstud2} we performed the change of variable $t = \frac{b}{s}$. In the final form of $p_{\bm{z}}(\bm{z})$ it is possible to recognize the kernel of a $k$-dimensional Student-$t$, $\bm{z} \sim \tstud{2 \alpha}{\bm{\mu}}{\frac{\beta}{\alpha} \bm{\Lambda}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Marginalize the joint density over $\sigma^2$ via the substitution $t=b/s$, yielding a Gamma integral whose form is the Student-$t$ kernel.

nodes.name: Marginalization over the variance
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} p_{\bm{z}}(\bm{z}) & = \int_{0}^{\infty} p_{(\bm{z}, \sigma^2)}(\bm{z}, \sigma^2) d \sigma^2 = \\ & \propto \int_{0}^{\infty} \exp{-\frac{1}{2 \sigma^2} \left(2 \beta + (\bm{z} - \bm{\mu})^T \bm{\Lambda}^{-1} (\bm{z} - \bm{\mu})\right)} \left(\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\right)^{\alpha + \frac{k}{2} + 1} d \sigma^2. \end{aligned}

nodes.label: eq:ninvgstud2

nodes.name: Sup norm and Lipschitz constant of the Gaussian likelihood
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{L}$ be a Gaussian likelihood, $\mathcal{L} \sim \normal{\bm{z}}{\sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2 \bm{I}_{n_L \times k}}$, it holds \begin{equation*} \norm{\mathcal{L}}_{\infty} = \frac{1}{\left(2 \pi \sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2\right)^{n_L k / 2}} \quad \text{and} \quad \lipschitz{\mathcal{L}} = \frac{e^{-1/2}}{\sqrt{\sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2}} \frac{1}{\left(2 \pi \sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2\right)^{n_L k / 2}}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Posterior BNN close to posterior NNGP, fixed variance (Trevisan Corollary 5.3)
nodes.statement: Given $f_{\bm{\theta}}$ BNN, with architecture $\bm{\alpha} = (\bm{n}, \bm{\varphi})$, $\bm{\varphi}$ collection of Lipschitz activation functions, prior distribution on $\bm{\theta}$ as in \cref{eq:nealprior}, $G$ Gaussian process as in \cref{eq:nngp}, $\bm{x}$, $\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$ as in \Cref{subsec:postbnn}, and a Gaussian likelihood function $\mathcal{L} \sim \normal{\bm{z}}{\sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2 \bm{I}_{n_L \times k}}$, exists a constant \begin{equation*} c\left(\mathcal{D}, \bm{\varphi}, \bm{\sigma}, \sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2, n_L\right) > 0, \text{ independent of } \left(n_l\right)_{l = 1}^{L - 1}, \end{equation*} such that, \begin{equation*} \wass[1]{f_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{x}) \, | \, \mathcal{D}}{G(\bm{x}) \, | \, \mathcal{D}} \leq c \frac{1}{\sqrt{n_{min}}}, \end{equation*} for all $\displaystyle n_{min} \coloneqq \min_{l = 1, \dots, L - 1} n_l$ sufficiently large.

conclusions: for all $\displaystyle n_{min} \coloneqq \min_{l = 1, \dots, L - 1} n_l$ sufficiently large

nodes.statement: The proof is straightforward if we observe that, by construction (see \cref{eq:nn,eq:nngpx}) $f_{\bm{\theta}} = \sigma f_{\bm{\theta}'}$ and $G = \sigma G'$, with \begin{equation} \bm{\theta}' \text{ such that } \bm{\sigma}' = \left(\left(\left(\sigma_{\bm{W}^{(l)}}^2, \sigma_{\bm{b}^{(l)}}^2\right)\right)_{l = 1}^{L - 1}, (1, 1)\right), \end{equation} and $G'$ built with weights and bias variances as in $\bm{\sigma}'$. \\ Indeed, applying \cref{eq:wasslinear} and \Cref{thm:priornngp} we get \begin{equation*} \wass[p]{f_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{x}) \, | \, \sigma^2}{G(\bm{x}) \, | \, \sigma^2} =\sigma \wass[p]{f_{\bm{\theta}}'(\bm{x})}{G'(\bm{x})} \leq \sigma c \sqrt{n_L} \sum_{l = 1}^{L - 1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{n_L}}, \end{equation*} with $c$ independent of $\sigma^2$.

nodes.statement: Unfortunately the second step is not easy as it could seem since \Cref{prop:wassconvexity} requires two families of probability measures (in particular Markov kernels) integrated with respect to the same measure $\nu$, which is not exactly our setting. Let us describe the issue before approaching the solution. For this purpose it is useful to introduce \begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} \mathit{I}_{\sigma^2}(s) \coloneqq \int_{\mathbb{R}^{n_L \times k}} \mathcal{L}(\bm{z}, s) \mu(d\bm{z}), \quad \widetilde{\mathit{I}}_{\sigma^2}(s) \coloneqq \int_{\mathbb{R}^{n_L \times k}} \mathcal{L}(\bm{z}, s) \widetilde{\mu}(d\bm{z}), \end{aligned} \end{equation*} which allow us to write, $\forall\,\,\,\, A \in \borel{\mathbb{R}^{n_L \times k}}$, \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & \mu_{\mathrm{post}}(A) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^+} \mu_{\sigma^2}(s)(A) \frac{\mathit{I}_{\sigma^2}(s)}{\mathit{I}} p_{\sigma^2}(s) ds, \text{ with } \mu_{\sigma^2}(s)(A) \coloneqq \int_A \frac{\mathcal{L}(\bm{z}, s) \mu(d\bm{z})}{\mathit{I}_{\sigma^2}(s)}, \\ & \widetilde{\mu}_{\mathrm{post}}(A) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^+} \widetilde{\mu}_{\sigma^2}(s)(A) \frac{\widetilde{\mathit{I}}_{\sigma^2}(s)}{\widetilde{\mathit{I}}} p_{\sigma^2}(s) ds, \text{ with } \widetilde{\mu}_{\sigma^2}(s)(A) \coloneqq \int_A \frac{\mathcal{L}(\bm{z}, s) \widetilde{\mu}(d\bm{z})}{\widetilde{\mathit{I}}_{\sigma^2}(s)}. \end{aligned} \end{equation} Eventually, we can note that the two families $(\mu_{\sigma^2}(s))_{s \in \mathbb{R}^+}$ and $(\widetilde{\mu}_{\sigma^2}(s))_{s \in \mathbb{R}^S}$, which coincide respectively with $\left(\mathbb{P}_{G(\bm{x}) \, | \, (\mathcal{D}, \sigma^2)}\right)_{\sigma^2 \in \mathbb{R}^+}$ and $\left(\mathbb{P}_{f_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{x}) \, | \, (\mathcal{D}, \sigma^2)}\right)_{\sigma^2 \in \mathbb{R}^+}$, are integrated with respect to different measures. Hence, it is clear that to apply \cref{eq:wassconvex} it is necessary to use the triangle inequality, \begin{equation} \wass[1]{\mu_{\mathrm{post}}}{\widetilde{\mu}_{\mathrm{post}}} \leq \wass[1]{\mu_{\mathrm{post}}}{\bar{\mu}} + \wass[1]{\bar{\mu}}{\widetilde{\mu}_{\mathrm{post}}}, \end{equation} where we inserted a third measure, \begin{equation} \bar{\mu}(A) \coloneqq \int_{\mathbb{R}^+} \widetilde{\mu}_{\sigma^2}(s)(A) \frac{\mathit{I}_{\sigma^2}(s)}{\mathit{I}} p_{\sigma^2}(s) ds, \ \forall\,\,\,\, A \in \borel{\mathbb{R}^{n_L \times k}}, \end{equation} specifically constructed to satisfy the hypothesis of the convexity property. \\ Now, to conclude, we just need to control both the terms on the right-hand side of \cref{eq:trianstep}.

nodes.statement: Given the Bayesian framework presented in \cref{eq:hiervariancenngp,eq:hiermodel,eq:rescaledkernel}, in order to get the posterior distribution of $G(\bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}}) \, | \, \mathcal{D}$ we write explicitly all the densities and apply the Bayes rule. In particular, assuming $\bm{K}'(\bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}}) \in \operatorname{Sym}_+^{k}$ invertible (we already know that is symmetric positive semi-definite), flattening all the random matrices by columns and defining \begin{equation*} \bm{y}_{\mathrm{f}} \coloneqq \flatten{\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}}, \quad \bm{z}_{\mathrm{f}} \coloneqq \flatten{\bm{z}}, \end{equation*} with $\bm{z} \coloneqq G(\bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}}) \in \mathbb{R}^{n_L \times k}$, we get \begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} p_{G(\bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}}) | \sigma^2}(\bm{z}) & = \frac{1}{\left((2\pi \sigma^2)^{n_L k} \det{\bm{K}'(\bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}}) \otimes_K \bm{I}_{n_L}}\right)^{1/2}} \cdot \\ & \kern14.65pt \cdot \exp{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \bm{z}_{\mathrm{f}}^T \left(\bm{K}'(\bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}}) \otimes_K \bm{I}_{n_L}\right)^{-1} \bm{z}_{\mathrm{f}}}, \\ p_{\sigma^2}(\sigma^2) & = \frac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)} \frac{1}{\left(\sigma^2\right)^{a + 1}} \exp{-\frac{b}{\sigma^2}}, \\ p_{\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}} | G(\bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}}), \sigma^2}(\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}) &= \frac{1}{\left(2\pi\sigma^2\right)^{n_L k / 2}} \exp{-\frac{1}{2 \sigma^2} (\bm{y}_{\mathrm{f}} - \bm{z}_{\mathrm{f}})^T (\bm{y}_{\mathrm{f}} - \bm{z}_{\mathrm{f}})}. \end{aligned} \end{equation*} with $\otimes_K$ representing the Kronecker product.

nodes.statement: By performing explicit computation we retrieve the posterior distribution of $G(\bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}}), \sigma^2 \, | \, \mathcal{D}$ as \begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} p_{G(\bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}}), \sigma^2 | \mathcal{D}}(\bm{z}, \sigma^2) & \propto p_{\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}} | G(\bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}}), \sigma^2}(\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}) \, p_{G(\bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}}) | \sigma^2}(\bm{z}) \, p_{\sigma^2}(\sigma^2) \propto \\ & \propto \frac{1}{\left(\sigma^2\right)^{n_L k / 2}} \exp{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} (\bm{y}_{\mathrm{f}} - \bm{z}_{\mathrm{f}})^T (\bm{y}_{\mathrm{f}} - \bm{z}_{\mathrm{f}})} \cdot \\ & \kern14.65pt \cdot \frac{1}{\left(\sigma^2\right)^{n_L k / 2} \sqrt{\det{\bm{K}'(\bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}})}}} \exp{-\frac{1}{2 \sigma^2} \bm{z}_{\mathrm{f}}^T \left(\bm{K}'(\bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}}) \otimes_K \bm{I}_{n_L}\right)^{-1} \bm{z}_{\mathrm{f}}} \cdot \\ & \kern14.65pt \cdot \frac{1}{\left(\sigma^2\right)^{a + 1}} \exp{-\frac{b}{\sigma^2}}. \end{aligned} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Substitute to get the joint posterior (28) and identify Gaus
nodes.statement: Substituting and multiplying for the constant term $\sqrt{\det{\bm{M}^{-1}}}$ we obtain \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} p_{G(\bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}}), \sigma^2 | \mathcal{D}}(\bm{z}, \sigma^2) & \propto \frac{1}{\left(\sigma^2\right)^{n_L k / 2} \sqrt{\det{\bm{M}^{-1}}}} \exp{-\frac{1}{2 \sigma^2} (\bm{z}_{\mathrm{f}} - \bm{M}^{-1} \bm{y}_{\mathrm{f}})^T \bm{M} (\bm{z}_{\mathrm{f}} - \bm{M}^{-1} \bm{y}_{\mathrm{f}})} \cdot \\ & \kern14.65pt \cdot \frac{1}{\left(\sigma^2\right)^{(a + n_L k / 2) + 1}} \exp{-\frac{1}{\sigma^2} \left(b + \frac{1}{2} \left(\bm{y}_{\mathrm{f}}^T \left(\bm{I}_{n_L k} - \bm{M}^{-1}\right) \bm{y}_{\mathrm{f}}\right)\right)}. \end{aligned} \end{equation} From \cref{eq:marginalposteriors} it is possible to identify two kernels: one associable with a Gaussian density and the other with an Inverse-Gamma density, \begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} \flatten{G(\bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}})} \, | \, \sigma^2, \mathcal{D} & \sim \normal{\bm{M}^{-1} \flatten{\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}}}{\sigma^2 \bm{M}^{-1}}, \\ \sigma^{2} \, | \, \mathcal{D} & \sim \invgamma{a + \frac{n_L k}{2}}{b + \frac{1}{2} \left(\flatten{\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}}^T \left(\bm{I}_{n_1 k} - \bm{M}^{-1}\right) \flatten{\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}}\right)}. \end{aligned} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Substitute to get the joint posterior (28) and identify Gaussian and Inverse-Gamma kernels

nodes.name: Apply Lemma B.1 to conclude the posterior is Student-$t$
nodes.statement: This result allows us to apply the following \Cref{lem:norminvgammastudent} (see \citet{bayesiantheory2009}) and state that the induced posterior distribution, $G(\bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}}) \, | \, \mathcal{D}$ is a $(n_L \times k)$-dimensional Student-$t$: \begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} \flatten{G(\bm{x}_{\mathcal{D}})} \, | \, \mathcal{D} \sim \tstud{2a + n_L k}{\bm{\mu}_{\mathrm{post}}}{\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{post}}}, \end{aligned} \end{equation*} with \begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} \bm{M} & \coloneqq \bm{I}_{n_L k} + \left(\bm{K}'(\bm{x}) \otimes_K \bm{I}_{n_L}\right)^{-1}, \\ \bm{\mu}_{\mathrm{post}} & \coloneqq \bm{M}^{-1} \flatten{\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}}, \\ \bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{post}} & \coloneqq \left(b + \frac{1}{2} \left(\flatten{\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}}^T \left(\bm{I}_{n_L k} - \bm{M}^{-1}\right) \flatten{\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}}\right)\right) \frac{2}{2a + n_L k} \bm{M}^{-1}. \end{aligned} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma B.1 to conclude the posterior is Student-$t$

nodes.name: Write the joint Gaussian-Inverse-Gamma density
nodes.statement: We know, by hypothesis that $(\bm{z}, \sigma^2)$ is such that \begin{align*} p_{(\bm{z}, \sigma^2)}(\bm{z}, \sigma^2) & = \frac{1}{(2 \pi)^{\frac{k}{2}} \left(\sigma^2\right)^{\frac{k}{2}} \sqrt{\det{\bm{\Lambda}}}} \exp{-\frac{1}{2 \sigma^2} (\bm{z} - \bm{\mu})^T \bm{\Lambda}^{-1} (\bm{z} - \bm{\mu})} \cdot \\ & \kern14.65pt \cdot \frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)} \left(\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\right)^{\alpha + 1} \exp{-\frac{\beta}{\sigma^2}}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Write the joint Gaussian-Inverse-Gamma density

nodes.name: Marginalize over $\sigma^2$
nodes.statement: Marginalizing over the variance $\sigma^2$ we get \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} p_{\bm{z}}(\bm{z}) & = \int_{0}^{\infty} p_{(\bm{z}, \sigma^2)}(\bm{z}, \sigma^2) d \sigma^2 = \\ & \propto \int_{0}^{\infty} \exp{-\frac{1}{2 \sigma^2} \left(2 \beta + (\bm{z} - \bm{\mu})^T \bm{\Lambda}^{-1} (\bm{z} - \bm{\mu})\right)} \left(\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\right)^{\alpha + \frac{k}{2} + 1} d \sigma^2. \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Marginalize over $\sigma^2$

nodes.name: Substitute $t=b/s$ to evaluate a Gamma integral
nodes.statement: Setting $a = \alpha + \frac{k}{2}$, $b = \frac{2 \beta + (\bm{z} - \bm{\mu})^T \bm{\Lambda}^{-1} (\bm{z} - \bm{\mu})}{2}$, $s = \sigma^2$ one can rewrite the last line of \cref{eq:ninvgstud1} as \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} p_{\bm{z}}(\bm{z}) & \propto \int_{0}^{\infty} s^{-(a + 1)} \exp{-\frac{b}{s}} d s = \int_{\infty}^{0} \left(\frac{t}{b}\right)^{a + 1} e^{-t} \left(-\frac{b}{t^2}\right) dt = \\ & = \int_{0}^{\infty} b^{-a} t^{a - 1} e^{-t} dt = \Gamma(a) b^{-a} \propto \left(\frac{2 \beta + (\bm{z} - \bm{\mu})^T \bm{\Lambda}^{-1} (\bm{z} - \bm{\mu})}{2}\right)^{-\left(\alpha + \frac{k}{2}\right)} \propto \\ & \propto \left(1 + \frac{1}{2 \alpha} (\bm{z} - \bm{\mu})^T \left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha} \bm{\Lambda}\right)^{-1} (\bm{z} - \bm{\mu})\right)^{-\frac{2\alpha + k}{2}}, \end{aligned} \end{equation} where in the first equality of \cref{eq:ninvgstud2} we performed the change of variable $t = \frac{b}{s}$.
nodes.statement_short: Substitute $t=b/s$ to evaluate a Gamma integral

nodes.name: Recognize the Student-$t$ kernel
nodes.statement: In the final form of $p_{\bm{z}}(\bm{z})$ it is possible to recognize the kernel of a $k$-dimensional Student-$t$, $\bm{z} \sim \tstud{2 \alpha}{\bm{\mu}}{\frac{\beta}{\alpha} \bm{\Lambda}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Recognize the Student-$t$ kernel

nodes.name: Rewrite the likelihood via the Frobenius norm
nodes.statement: We first rewrite the map in a more compact form in terms of the Frobenius norm of $(\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}} - \bm{z})$: $\forall\,\,\,\, \bm{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_L \times k}$, \begin{equation*} \mathcal{L}(\bm{z}; \bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}) = \frac{1}{\left(2 \pi \sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2\right)^{n_L k / 2}} \exp{-\frac{1}{2\sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2} \norm{\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}} - \bm{z}}_F^2}. \end{equation*}

nodes.statement: Then for the uniform norm it is sufficient to recall that $\mathcal{L}$ is a bell-shaped map with maximum in the mean point. Hence, our objective is to identify the value of $\sup_{\bm{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_L \times k}} \norm{\partial / \partial \bm{z} \, \mathcal{L}(\bm{z}; \bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}})}_F$.

nodes.name: Introduce the radial function $l$ with $l(\|y-z\|_F)=h(z)$ a
nodes.statement: It is also possible to define \begin{equation*} l: \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}, \ l(x) \coloneqq \frac{x}{\sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2} \frac{1}{\left(2 \pi \sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2\right)^{n_L k / 2}} \exp{-\frac{1}{2 \sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2} x^2}, \ \forall\,\,\,\, x \in \mathbb{R}^+, \end{equation*} which, by construction, has the following property: \begin{equation*} \forall\,\,\,\, \bm{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_L \times k}, \ l(\norm{\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}} - \bm{z}}_F) = h(\bm{z}). \end{equation*} From the definition it is easy to see that $\sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}^+} l(x) = h(\bm{z}_0)$, just computing its first two derivatives $l'$ and $l''$. Defining $d = \sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^{-2} \left(2 \pi \sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2\right)^{- n_L k / 2}$ positive constant we have \begin{align*} l'(x) & = d \exp{-\frac{1}{2\sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2} x^2} \left(1 - x^2 \frac{1}{\sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2}\right), \\ l''(x) & = - d \exp{-\frac{1}{2\sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2} x^2} \frac{1}{\sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2} x \left(\left(1 - x^2 \frac{1}{\sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2}\right) + 2\right) = \\ & = - d \exp{-\frac{1}{2\sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2} x^2} \frac{1}{\sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2} x \left(3 - \frac{x^2}{\sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2}\right), \end{align*} and so \begin{align*} l'(x) = 0 \iff x^2 = \sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2, \ l''(x) \leq 0 \iff x^2 \leq 3 \sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2. \end{align*}

nodes.name: The critical value is the global maximum, giving the Lipschi
nodes.statement: This implies that in $x = \sqrt{\sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2}$ there is a local maximum and observing the asymptotic behavior, $\lim_{x \to +\infty} l(x) = 0$, we know that it is the unique global maximum. Finally, evaluating $l$ in $\sqrt{\sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2}$ we get \begin{equation*} l\left(\sqrt{\sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2}\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2}} \frac{e^{- 1/2}}{\left(2 \pi \sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2\right)^{n_L k / 2}}. \end{equation*} Therefore, it follows that the critical points $\bm{z}_0$ are global maxima for $h$ and so \begin{equation*} \sup_{\bm{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_L \times k}} \norm{\frac{\partial}{\partial \bm{z}} \mathcal{L}(\bm{z}; \bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}})}_F = h(\bm{z}_0). \end{equation*}

Due to the boundedness and positivity of $\mathcal{L}: \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out} \times k}} \to (0, \norm{\mathcal{L}}_{\infty})$, it is clear that $p^{(1)} \in (0, \infty)$, indeed we are integrating $\mathcal{L}$ with respect to a strictly positive probability measure: $0 < p^{(1)}(\mathcal{D}, \bm{\varphi}, \bm{\sigma}, \sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2, n_L) =$ $= \mean{\mathcal{L}(G(\bm{x}); \bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}})} \leq \norm{\mathcal{L}}_{\infty}$.

nodes.statement: Moreover, it is possible to notice that considering $\bm{v} \sim G(\bm{x})$, $\bm{w} \sim f_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{x})$, \begin{align*} |p^{(1)} - p^{(2)}| & = \left|\mean{\mathcal{L}(\bm{v}; \bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}) - \mathcal{L}(\bm{w}; \bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}})}\right| \leq \norm{\mathcal{L}(\bm{v}; \bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}) - \mathcal{L}(\bm{w}; \bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}})}_{L^1} \leq \lipschitz{\mathcal{L}} \norm{\bm{v} - \bm{w}}_{L^1}, \end{align*} and taking the infimum over the couplings $(\bm{v}, \bm{w})$ we get \begin{align} |p^{(1)} - p^{(2)}| \leq \lipschitz{\mathcal{L}} \wass[1]{G(\bm{x})}{f_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{x})} \leq \lipschitz{\mathcal{L}} c_1 \frac{1}{\sqrt{n_{min}}}, \end{align} where for the last inequality we used a compact version of the result in \Cref{thm:priornngp}. Recalling that $c_1$ and $\lipschitz{\mathcal{L}}$ depend only on $\bm{x}, \bm{\varphi}, \bm{\sigma}, \sigma_{\scalebox{0.65}{$\kern-3pt\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}$}}^2$ and $n_L$, \cref{eq:p1-2} implies that, for $n_{min}$ sufficiently large, $p^{(2)}$ is also strictly positive.

nodes.name: Recall the characterization of total variation
nodes.statement: We use the following characterization of the total variation measure (see Section 6.1 of \citet{rcarudin1987}): $\forall\,\,\,\, A \in \borel{\mathbb{R}^S}$, \begin{equation*} |\mu - \nu|(A) = \sup_{\left(A_i\right)_{i = 1}^{\infty}, \ \bigsqcup_{i = 1}^{\infty} A_i = A} \sum_{i = 1}^{\infty} |(\mu - \nu)(A_i)|. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Recall the characterization of total variation

nodes.name: Introduce $k(s)$ and express $|\bar\mu-\widetilde\mu_{post}|
nodes.statement: Now the problem is that we do not know how to measure maps with the finite measure $|\bar{\mu} - \widetilde{\mu}_\mathrm{post}|$, but we know how to bound it. \\ Indeed, introducing the following notation to improve the readability, \begin{equation*} k(s) \coloneqq \frac{\mathit{I}_{\sigma^2}(s)}{\mathit{I}} - \frac{\widetilde{\mathit{I}}_{\sigma^2}(s)}{\widetilde{\mathit{I}}}, \end{equation*} we have \begin{equation*} \bar{\mu} - \widetilde{\mu}_{\mathrm{post}} = \int_{\mathbb{R}^+} k(s) \widetilde{\mu}_{\sigma^2}(s) p_{\sigma^2}(s) ds, \end{equation*} and therefore $\forall\,\,\,\, A \in \borel{\mathbb{R}^{n_L \times k}}$, \begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} |\bar{\mu} - \widetilde{\mu}_\mathrm{post}|(A) & = \sup_{\left(A_i\right)_{i = 1}^{\infty}, \ \bigsqcup_{i = 1}^{\infty} A_i = A} \sum_{i = 1}^{\infty} \left|\int_{\mathbb{R}^+} k(s) \widetilde{\mu}_{\sigma^2}(s)(A_i) p_{\sigma^2}(s) ds\right| \leq \\ & \leq \sup_{\left(A_i\right)_{i = 1}^{\infty}, \ \bigsqcup_{i = 1}^{\infty} A_i = A} \sum_{i = 1}^{\infty} \int_{\mathbb{R}^+} |k(s)| \widetilde{\mu}_{\sigma^2}(s)(A_i) p_{\sigma^2}(s) ds = \\ & = \sup_{\left(A_i\right)_{i = 1}^{\infty}, \ \bigsqcup_{i = 1}^{\infty} A_i = A} \lim_{j \to \infty} \int_{\mathbb{R}^+} |k(s)| \widetilde{\mu}_{\sigma^2}(s)\left(\bigsqcup_{i = 1}^j A_i\right) p_{\sigma^2}(s) ds. \end{aligned} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $k(s)$ and express $|\bar\mu-\widetilde\mu_{post}|$ through it

nodes.name: Dominated convergence bounds the total variation by a measur
nodes.statement: It is easy to observe that it is possible to apply Dominated Convergence Theorem: $\forall\,\,\,\, j \in \mathbb{N}_{> 0}$, \begin{equation*} \left||k(s)| \widetilde{\mu}_{\sigma^2}(s)\left(\bigsqcup_{i = 1}^j A_i\right) p_{\sigma^2}(s)\right| \leq |k(s)| p_{\sigma^2}(s) \quad \text{and} \quad \int_{\mathbb{R}^+} |k(s)| p_{\sigma^2}(s) \leq 2. \end{equation*} Therefore, \begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} |\bar{\mu} - \widetilde{\mu}_\mathrm{post}|(A) & \leq \sup_{\left(A_i\right)_{i = 1}^{\infty}, \ \bigsqcup_{i = 1}^{\infty} A_i = A} \int_{\mathbb{R}^+} |k(s)| \widetilde{\mu}_{\sigma^2}(s)\left(\bigsqcup_{i = 1}^\infty A_i\right) p_{\sigma^2}(s) ds = \\ & = \int_{\mathbb{R}^+} |k(s)| \widetilde{\mu}_{\sigma^2}(s)(A) p_{\sigma^2}(s) ds \eqcolon \nu(A). \end{aligned} \end{equation*} It is easy to observe that $\nu: \borel{\mathbb{R}^{n_L \times k}} \to \mathbb{R}^+$ is a finite measure, indeed:
nodes.statement_short: Dominated convergence bounds the total variation by a measure $\nu$, which is finite

nodes.statement: Let us thus prove \cref{eq:boundks}. We begin by observing that we already know how to bound the absolute difference $\big|\mathit{I}_{\sigma^2}(s) - \widetilde{\mathit{I}}_{\sigma^2}(s)\big|$, using the same arguments applied in the proof of \Cref{lem:boundexplikelihood}: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \left|\mathit{I}_{\sigma^2}(s) - \widetilde{\mathit{I}}_{\sigma^2}(s)\right| & \leq \lipschitz{\mathcal{L}(\cdot, s)} \wass[1]{G(\bm{x})}{f_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{x})} \leq c s^{-n_L k / 2 - 1/2} \cdot s^{1/2} \frac{c}{\sqrt{n_{min}}} \leq \\ & \leq s^{- n_L k /2} \frac{c}{\sqrt{n_{min}}}. \end{aligned} \end{equation} Therefore, it remains to show that $\mathit{I}^{-1} \leq c$ and $\widetilde{\mathit{I}}^{-1} \geq c$ for some $c$ depending only on the usual parameters. Indeed, it would yield \begin{equation*} \left|\frac{\mathit{I}_{\sigma^2}(s)}{\mathit{I}} - \frac{\widetilde{\mathit{I}}_{\sigma^2}(s)}{\widetilde{\mathit{I}}}\right| \leq c \left|\mathit{I}_{\sigma^2}(s) - \widetilde{\mathit{I}}_{\sigma^2}(s)\right| \leq s^{- n_L k /2} \frac{c}{\sqrt{n_{min}}}. \end{equation*} We already saw $\mathit{I} \geq c$ in \cref{eq:lowerboundI}, but in order to find an upper bound for $\widetilde{\mathit{I}}$ we also need an upper bound for $\mathit{I}$. The procedure to get it is analogous to the one used in \cref{eq:lowerboundI}: starting from \Cref{lem:boundexplikelihood} we bound the negative exponential with $1$, and we are done, \begin{align*} \mathit{I} & \leq c \int_{\mathbb{R}^+} s^{-n_L k / 2} \exp{-\frac{1}{s} \frac{\varepsilon}{2 (\varepsilon + 1)} \norm{\bm{y}_{\mathcal{D}}}_F^2} p_{\sigma^2}(s) ds \leq c \int_{\mathbb{R}^+} s^{-n_L k / 2 - a - 1} \exp{-\frac{b}{s}} ds = \\ & = c \Gamma\left(n_L k / 2 + a\right). \end{align*} To prove $\widetilde{\mathit{I}} \leq c$ it is sufficient to observe that \begin{align*} \left|\mathit{I} - \widetilde{\mathit{I}}\right| & = \left|\int_{\mathbb{R}^+} \left(\mathit{I}_{\sigma^2}(s) - \widetilde{\mathit{I}}_{\sigma^2}(s)\right) p_{\sigma^2}(s) ds\right| \leq \int_{\mathbb{R}^+} \left|\mathit{I}_{\sigma^2}(s) - \widetilde{\mathit{I}}_{\sigma^2}(s)\right| p_{\sigma^2}(s) ds \leq \\ & \leq \frac{c}{\sqrt{n_{min}}} \int_{\mathbb{R}^+} s^{-n_L k / 2 - a - 1} \exp{-\frac{b}{s}} ds = \frac{c}{\sqrt{n_{min}}}, \end{align*} where from the 1\textsuperscript{st} to the 2\textsuperscript{nd} line we used the inequality in \cref{eq:absdiffIstildeIs}. Hence, considering $n_{min}$ sufficiently large to have $\sqrt{n_{min}} > 2c / \mathit{I}$, it follows $|\mathit{I} - \widetilde{\mathit{I}}| \leq \mathit{I} / 2$ which implies $\widetilde{\mathit{I}} \leq 3/2 \, \mathit{I} \leq c$.
